paras: The attempted lynching on a Norfolk trolley car was an attack in Norfolk, Virginia, on the night of February 9, 1919, in which enlisted navy men seized an unidentified Black man and tried to electrocute him on a streetcar's trolley wire. A petty officer stopped them and persuaded them to leave the matter to the police. Three Black newspapers carried the story, one headlining it an attempted lynching.

According to a Norfolk dispatch dated February 10, the trouble began on a crowded trolley car when an enlisted man, E. J. Hahn, tried to enforce the "Jim Crow" law. Hahn tried to eject a Black man from a front seat after the man refused to go to the rear of the car.

In the fight that followed, Hahn was slashed with a razor, and within minutes a dozen fights had broken out while passengers panicked. Sailors then seized a man they suspected of wielding the razor, tied him to the trolley pole of the car, and tried to lift him up to the trolley wire. A petty officer intervened and, by appeals, persuaded the men to let the police handle the situation.
The coverage does not report whether the man was arrested or charged, what became of Hahn's wound, or whether any of the sailors were disciplined.

The Cleveland Advocate printed the dispatch first, on February 15, under the headline "'Jack Tars' Attempt Lynching at Norfolk," naming the sailors' act a lynching attempt. Nearly a month later, on March 8, the New York Age ran the same text as a short item titled "Saved From Eleastrecution," placed inside a local column of news from Chambersburg, Pennsylvania. The same day the Philadelphia Tribune ran a front-page brief, "Defends Himself When Attacked by Sailors," which stressed that the man "used a razor very effectively" against his attackers.

The Tribune's brief carried the dateline "Mnr. 3," while the earlier Cleveland Advocate dispatch was dated February 10 and described events of the previous night. It also named "enlisted men of the Army" and a street corner, but its own headline speaks of sailors and its rescuer held a naval rank, so it likely garbles the same trolley incident.

reader.title: Attempted lynching on a Norfolk trolley car
bases: Enlisted sailors seized a Black man suspected of a razor cutting, tied him to a trolley pole and tried to lift him to the trolley wire before a petty officer stopped them; the Cleveland Advocate headlined it an attempted lynching (A1, A2).
All three reports appear to derive from one Norfolk dispatch: A2 repeats A1's wording, and A3 is a condensed, garbled version; no independent local or follow-up report was found (A1, A2, A3).

accounts.label: Norfolk dispatch (Feb. 10)
accounts.gist: A Jim Crow seating dispute on a crowded trolley became a free-for-all; after a razor cutting, sailors tied a suspected Black man to the trolley pole and tried to lift him to the wire until a petty officer intervened.

accounts.label: Philadelphia Tribune brief
accounts.gist: An unknown Black man used a razor to defend himself when a mob of Army enlisted men attacked him on a street corner, and a petty officer rescued him.

framing.detail: The Cleveland Advocate headlined the story '"Jack Tars" Attempt Lynching at Norfolk', naming the sailors' act a lynching attempt.
The New York Age ran the dispatch as a short item, 'Saved From Eleastrecution', tucked inside a Chambersburg, Pa. local column.
The Philadelphia Tribune's front-page headline 'Defends Himself When Attacked by Sailors' cast the man as defending himself against a mob.

sources.note: Fullest account, datelined Norfolk Feb. 10: sailors tied a Black man to a trolley pole and tried to lift him to the wire after a Jim Crow seating fight; a petty officer intervened.
quotes: Only the timely appeal of a petty officers last night prevented angry enlisted men of the navy from electrocuting an unknown Colored man
The cutting occurred during a free-for-all fight on a crowded trolley car that resulted when Hahn attempted to enforce the "Jim Crow" law.
Sailors seized a man suspected of being the wielder of the razor, tied him to the trolley pole of the car, and were endeavoring to lift him up to the trolley wire
